question: A suspected juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) should NEVER be biopsied in clinic because of the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage; the investigation of choice is contrast-enhanced CT or MRI of the nasopharynx.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true and describes a critical patient-safety rule. JNA = do NOT biopsy in clinic. The tumour's arterial supply (internal maxillary artery, often also internal carotid branches) makes incisional biopsy potentially fatal. Always image first (CT/MRI), then plan surgery with pre-operative embolisation.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. JNA is a highly vascular benign tumour arising from the sphenopalatine foramen in adolescent males. Biopsy in clinic risks uncontrollable arterial bleeding. The standard workup is contrast-enhanced CT (to assess bony erosion and tumour extent) and MRI (for soft tissue spread). Angiography is done pre-operatively for embolisation. This is one of the three 'never biopsy' rules in ENT.
